title: WoE in R with tidywoe
text:
WoE (weight of evidence) is a tool widely used in logistic regression applications, mainly in credit scoring. Simply put, it turns categories into numbers that reflect the difference between them by how well they separate Y = 1 from Y = 0.
If you don’t know what it is yet or want to read more about it, here is a text I enjoyed reading:
The author of this text is Kim Larsen, creator of the Information package, which is complete and full of sophisticated tools around WoE. However, in my day-to-day work every now and then I had to write my own routines to build the WoE versions of my variables, even with several complete packages available. The main reason was that they weren’t very practical and didn’t fit the tidyverse philosophy. So I ended up gathering these routines into a package called tidywoe and putting it out there. The idea is to help the analyst gain time, readability and reproducibility. Here is how to use it.

title: Untuned vs tuned xgboost, one tree at a time
text:
A while ago I posted on LinkedIn an “untuned vs tuned xgboost fit” GIF. This post rebuilds it from the original code, with both models side by side.
Both panels use the same data and the same algorithm. Only the hyperparameters differ. With the defaults, the curve takes big steps early on and then starts chasing the noise. With tuned hyperparameters, it moves to the sine in smaller steps and stays smooth.

title: Untuned vs tuned xgboost, one tree at a time
text:
The data

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(gganimate)
theme_set(theme_minimal(16))

set.seed(1)
dados <- tibble(
  x = runif(1000) - 0.5,
  y = sin(x * pi * 2) + rnorm(1000, sd = 0.3)
)

The noise has standard deviation 0.3, so no model can get a root mean squared error (RMSE) below about 0.3 on new data.

title: Untuned vs tuned xgboost, one tree at a time
text:
Two models
The tuned model uses the hyperparameters from the gist. The untuned one keeps boost_tree()’s defaults: 15 trees, tree_depth = 6 and learn_rate = 0.3. Both start from the same base_score, the mean of y.

trees <- 30

tuned <- boost_tree(
  mode = "regression",
  mtry = 1,
  trees = trees,
  min_n = 1,
  tree_depth = 4,
  learn_rate = 0.1,
  sample_size = 1,
  loss_reduction = 0.1
) %>%
  set_engine("xgboost", base_score = mean(dados$y))

untuned <- boost_tree(mode = "regression") %>%
  set_engine("xgboost", base_score = mean(dados$y))

ajustes <- list(
  untuned = fit(untuned, y ~ x, data = dados),
  tuned   = fit(tuned, y ~ x, data = dados)
)

title: Untuned vs tuned xgboost, one tree at a time
Untuned vs tuned xgboost, one tree at a time

The GIF
Same plot as the gist, with one panel per model.

gif <- df %>%

  geom_point(aes(y = y), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_function(fun = ~sin(. * pi * 2), colour = "purple", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_step(aes(y = pred), colour = "orange", linewidth = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ modelo) +
  transition_time(step) +
  labs(title = 'Step: {frame_time}') +

anim <- animate(gif, nframes = trees + 1 + 10, fps = 5, end_pause = 10, width = 1000, height = 450, units = "px", res = 100)
anim_save("xgboost.gif", anim)

title: Untuned vs tuned xgboost, one tree at a time
text:
How much better?
The GIF shows the difference. RMSE puts a number on it: on the training data, and on 5,000 new points from the same curve.

set.seed(2)
novos <- tibble(
  x = runif(5000) - 0.5,
  y = sin(x * pi * 2) + rnorm(5000, sd = 0.3)
)

rmse_de <- function(ajuste, d) rmse_vec(d$y, predict(ajuste, d)$.pred)

tibble(
  modelo = names(ajustes),
  rmse_treino = map_dbl(ajustes, rmse_de, dados),
  rmse_novos  = map_dbl(ajustes, rmse_de, novos)
) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

The untuned model has the lower error on the training data, below the 0.3 noise level, which means it fitted part of the noise. On new data the order flips and the tuned model wins.

title: Untuned vs tuned xgboost, one tree at a time
text:
Tuning for real
The hyperparameters above came with the gist. In practice you find them with cross-validation, for example with {tune}:

spec <- boost_tree(
  mode = "regression",
  trees = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), learn_rate = tune(), loss_reduction = tune()
) %>%
  set_engine("xgboost")

resultados <- tune_grid(spec, y ~ x, resamples = vfold_cv(dados, v = 5), grid = 20)
show_best(resultados, metric = "rmse")

Defaults are a starting point, not a model. Tune your models, folks!

title: Neural Style Transfer with Torch
text:
library(torch)
library(torchvision)
library(zeallot)
device <- torch_device(if(cuda_is_available()) "cuda" else "cpu")
cpu <- torch_device("cpu")
Neural Style Transfer is one of the most fun and “artistic” techniques in deep learning. The image below sums up what we are going to do.
You give the neural network two images, style and content, and the result is the content image in the style of style. It’s like an Instagram filter, but with the style of your favorite artist =P.
This post adapts to R + torch an exercise from the deeplearning.ai ‘Convolutional Neural Networks’ course that I took, originally in Python + tensorflow. When I started writing this post, I meant to make it as didactic as possible, but I don’t think I could beat the Coursera course, so I’ll stick to the main points and comment the code for anyone who wants to create their own images! Also, this video (in Portuguese) gives a summary of the NST strategy.
PS: while writing this post I found out that Daniel had already written a little NST example for torchvision. I stole part of the code from there haha.

title: Neural Style Transfer with Torch
text:
Key concepts and ideas
The idea is to generate a generated image G whose content is similar to content C and whose style is similar to style S. Content and style are usually extracted from a pre-trained convnet. The original paper (Gatys et al. 2015) uses VGG19, which already comes with {torchvision}.

# VGG19 model
vgg <- model_vgg19(pretrained = TRUE)$features$to(device = device)

# freezing the weights
vgg$parameters %>% purrr::walk(function(param) param$requires_grad_(FALSE))

So VGG19 will give us the features, and now we need to define cost functions to find the image with the best trade-off between the content of one image and the style of another. Building the algorithm can be split into three parts:

content cost function: \(L_{content}(C, G)\)
style cost function: \(L_{style}(S, G)\)
Overall cost function: \(L(G) = \alpha L_{content}(C, G) + \beta L_{style}(S, G)\)


content cost function
On choosing shallow versus deep layers:

The first layers of a convolutional network tend to extract more basic patterns, such as edges and simple textures.
Deeper layers usually capture more sophisticated features, such as detailed textures and objects.

As for picking a middle layer: we want the generated image to have content similar to content. The strategy is:

choose one layer of the network to represent this “content”.
take that layer for each of the content and generated images.
make the network force these two layers to be as similar as possible.

So the cost function that reflects point (3) can simply be the mean squared error between the pixels of that layer:

content_loss <- function(content_layer, generated_layer) {
  nnf_mse_loss(content_layer, generated_layer)
}

NOTE: In practice, you’ll get the “coolest” result if you choose layers from the middle: not too shallow, not too deep. Since VGG19 has 37 layers, the chosen one could be, for example, layer 14.


style cost function
The purpose of the style cost function is to minimize the distance between the so-called Gram matrices of the style and generated images.

Gram matrix
In the literature, the style matrix is called the Gram matrix. In mathematics, given a set of vectors, the Gram matrix is the matrix of the inner products of every pair of those vectors. It’s like a correlation matrix, but without centering by the mean. In practice, you take a layer of the network, reshape it into a 2D tensor (a matrix) and compute \(A * A^T\).

gram_matrix <- function(tensor) {
  c(b,c,h,w) %<-% tensor$size()
  tensor <- tensor$view(c(c, h*w))
  torch_matmul(tensor, tensor$t())/(h*w)
}

The cost function \(L_{style}(S, G)\) is the good old mean squared error between the Gram matrices.

style_loss <- function(style_layer, generated_layer) {
  style_gram <- gram_matrix(style_layer)
  generated_gram <- gram_matrix(generated_layer)
  nnf_mse_loss(style_gram, generated_gram)
}



Style layers
Instead of one, we take five intermediate layers of the network and compute the distances between their Gram matrices. The cost function then becomes a weighted sum of these five distances: \(L_{style}(S, G) = \sum_{l=1}^{5}\lambda^{[l]}L_{style}^{[l]}(S,G)\)

style_layers <- c(2, 7, 12, 21, 29) # choice of VGG layers
lambdas <- 1e5/(c(1,10,10,10,10)^2) # weights for each layer in the final style

Now it’s worth creating an nn_module() that returns the intermediate layers of the network (VGG19, in this case). The layers_out argument lets us choose which layers we want back.

features <- nn_module(
  initialize = function(convnet) {
    # could be any pre-trained convnet. We'll use VGG19
    self$convnet <- convnet
  },
  forward = function(img, layers_out = NULL) {
    layers <- seq_along(self$convnet) # 1 to 37
    if(is.null(layers_out)) layers_out <- layers
    conv_outs <- purrr::accumulate(layers, ~self$convnet[[.y]](.x), .init = img) # list of 37 tensors
    conv_outs[layers_out] # list with only the selected layers
  }
)

title: Neural Style Transfer with Torch
text:
Optimization
Below is the commented code to run the optimization.

# helper functions
to_r <- function(x) as.numeric(x$to(device = cpu))

plot_image <- function(tensor) {
  im <- tensor$to(device = "cpu")[1,..]$
    permute(c(2, 3, 1))$
    to(device = "cpu")$
    clamp(0,1) %>% # make it [0,1]
    as.array()
  par(mar = c(0,0,0,0))
  plot(as.raster(im))
}

load_image <- function(path, geometry = "250x200") {
  img <- path %>%
    magick_loader() %>%
    magick::image_resize(geometry) %>%
    transform_to_tensor() %>%
    torch_unsqueeze(1)

  img$to(device = device)
}

The parameters and inputs worth experimenting with are:

content and style: the input images, one for content and one for style.
content_layer: the VGG19 layer used to extract the content of the content image.
style_layers: the VGG19 layers used to extract the style of the style image.
lambdas: the weight of each style feature in the optimization.
content_weight: the weight of the content features in the optimization.
style_weight: the (overall) weight of the style features in the optimization.

Two other parameters that drastically affect the result are the dimensions of the two input images. In the code below, "400x400" and "350x500" can be swapped for other dimensions to get different results.
While creating, you’ll be tweaking these parameters all the time!

# INPUT: content and style images
content <- load_image("content/posts/2021-02-22-neural-style-transfer/cristoredentor3.jpg", "400x400")
style <- load_image("content/posts/2021-02-22-neural-style-transfer/vangogh_starry_night.jpg", "350x500")

# style and content feature setup
content_layer <- 14
style_layers <- c(2, 7, 12, 21, 29)
lambdas <- 1e5/(c(1,10,10,10,10)^2)
content_weight <- 2
style_weight <- 4e-1




content





style



# FEATURES: extracted from VGG19
vgg_features <- features(vgg)
content_features <- vgg_features(content, content_layer)
style_features <- vgg_features(style, style_layers)

# OUTPUT: generated image
generated <- torch_clone(content)$requires_grad_(TRUE)
optim <- optim_adam(generated, lr = 0.02)
lr_scheduler <- lr_step(optim, 100, 0.9)

# optimization loop
for(step in seq_len(8000)) {
  optim$zero_grad()
  # update the features of the image being generated
  generated_features <- vgg_features(generated, c(content_layer, style_layers))

  # losses
  LC <- content_loss(content_features[[1]], generated_features[[1]])
  LS <- 0
  for(i in seq_along(lambdas))
    LS <- LS + lambdas[i]*style_loss(style_features[[i]], generated_features[-1][[i]])

  loss <- content_weight * LC + style_weight * LS

  loss$backward()
  optim$step()
  lr_scheduler$step()

  # feedback
  if(step %% 100 == 0) {
    cat(glue::glue("LC = {to_r(LC)} - LS = {to_r(LS)} - Loss = {to_r(loss)}\n\n"))
    plot_image(generated)
  }
}

# final image

title: Logistic Regression in: the world’s smallest deep learning
text:
Motivation
I read statisticians, computer scientists, data engineers and the like questioning the future of Machine Learning and whether everything we knew before about statistical modeling had become obsolete (like this question on Quora: Should I Quit Machine Learning?).
And in conversations with people close to me I noticed some excitement about the novelty and frustration with the “obsolescence” of what they had spent time studying before.
To make it worse, opportunists rode this wave to do malicious marketing aimed at devaluing and dividing the data analyst community. Something very similar to what happened with other buzzwords like data science, big data, Python versus R and machine learning itself. Before, there was the classic advertising that company X used MACHINE LEARNING instead of predictive models. Now things have evolved and they resort to the word Deep Learning.
What really matters:

Deep Learning is big news and has put Artificial Intelligence in the spotlight.
Whoever knew Machine Learning before will be able to apply 95% of their knowledge in Deep Learning applications (including bayesianism, bootstrap, inference, probability and the whole lot).
Deep Learning has to be seen as one more tool in the data analyst’s toolbox, not a replacement.

And to address this question I decided to fit a logistic regression using deep learning so that everyone who has ever fit a logistic regression can say they have built a neural network too! I confess a slightly provocative motivation, but what fun would it be otherwise? =P

title: Logistic Regression in: the world’s smallest deep learning
text:
What we’ll do

Logistic regression for \(Y_1\) (with glm)
Deep Learning for \(Y_1\) (with keras)
Show that logistic regression is not the best for \(Y_2\) and that Deep Learning goes beyond the limitation of linear models (with glm)
Deep Learning for \(Y_2\) (with keras)

Let’s get to work.

Packages

library(keras)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(forcats)
library(ggplot2)

title: Logistic Regression in: the world’s smallest deep learning
text:
Logistic regression versus Deep Learning
Time to fit models to the same data in two different ways: logistic regression with glm and deep learning with keras.

Simulated data

logit <- function(p) log(p) - log(1 - p)
logistic <- function(x) 1/(1 + exp(-x))

n <- 100000
set.seed(19880923)
df <- data_frame(x = runif(n, -2, 2.5)) %>%
  mutate(y_1 = rbinom(n, 1, prob = logistic(-1 + 2 * x)), # y_1
         y_2 = rbinom(n, 1, prob = logistic(-1 + 2 * tanh(-1 + 2 * x)))) # y_2

The code above created two response variables (targets). In mathematical notation, they are defined as follows:
Response y_1
\[E[Y_1|x] = \text{logistic}{(-1 + 2x)} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{{-(-1 + 2x)}}}\]
Response y_2
\[E[Y_2|x] = \text{logistic}{(-1 + 2\tanh(-1 + 2x))} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{{-(-1 + 2\tanh(-1 + 2x))}}}\]
\(x\) is linear in the logit of y_1, so logistic regression will do well at finding the parameters \(-1\) and \(2\). However, \(x\) is not linear in the logit of y_2, so logistic regression won’t be able to faithfully represent the generator of y_2.
NOTE 1: The form \(\text{logistic}{(\beta_0 + \beta_1\tanh(\beta_2 + \beta_3X))}\) has parameters inside the tanh function, which means our hypothesis for \(E[Y_2|x]\) is no longer linear in the parameters. That’s why linear models (as the name suggests) are no longer suitable. And non-linearity is one of the generalizations neural networks give us! (yes, this is very relevant)
NOTE 2: of course, in this very simple one-variable case we could inspect the data to find good transformations of \(x\) so that the logistic fit would be as good as a neural network’s, but if we added many other variables things would get complicated!
In neural network notation, the formulas above look like this:
Response y_1









Response y_2









What was a link function in GLM became an activation function in neural networks (at the end I talk more about vocabulary that changed).


A look at the data

# skimr::skim(df) %>% skim_print %>% with(numeric)  %>% mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 2) %>% DT::datatable()

df %>%
  gather(y_id, y_val, y_1, y_2) %>%
  mutate(x_cat = cut_number(x, n = 70)) %>%
  group_by(x_cat, y_id) %>%
  summarise(p = mean(y_val),
            n = n()) %>%
  mutate(logit_p = logit(p)) %>%
  gather(transformacao, p, p, logit_p) %>%
  mutate(transformacao = transformacao %>% fct_inorder %>% fct_recode("logit(p)" = "logit_p")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = x_cat, y = p, colour = y_id)) +
  theme_minimal(20) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~forcats::fct_inorder(transformacao), nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "x", colour = "resposta") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank())
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'x_cat'. You can override using the
## `.groups` argument.








The plot on the right shows that x is proportional to the logit of the probabilities of y_1 (in red), as it should be since we built it that way. With y_2 (in blue), it still looks like a sigmoid even after the transformation.


Fitting the models

Logistic regression for \(Y_1\) (with glm)

# glm model 1 -------------------------------------------------------
modelo_glm_1 <- glm(y_1 ~ x, data = df, family = binomial)


# coefficients
coef(modelo_glm_1)

# (Intercept)           x
#   -1.018434    2.011647

# accuracy
conf_matrix_glm_1 <- table(modelo_glm_1$fitted.values > 0.5, df$y_1)
sum(diag(conf_matrix_glm_1))/sum(conf_matrix_glm_1)

# [1] 0.85061

The estimates came out very close to the true values \(\beta_0 = -1\) and \(\beta_1 = 2\).
The accuracy was 85%.


Deep Learning for \(Y_1\) (with keras)
Let’s build our hypothesis for \(E[Y_1|x]\).

# keras model 1 --------------------------------------------------------
# input: 1 variable: x.
input_keras_1 <- layer_input(1, name = "modelo_keras_1")

# output: there are no hidden layers, only the logit link function directly.
output_keras_1 <- input_keras_1 %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, name = "camada_unica") %>%
  layer_activation("sigmoid", input_shape = 1, name = "link_logistic") # sigmoid in tensorflow is the logistic

# keras_model is what builds our hypothesis f(x) (from E[y] = f(x))
modelo_keras_1 <- keras_model(input_keras_1, output_keras_1)

#
summary(modelo_keras_1)

Model
_____________________________________________________________
Layer (type)                     Output Shape    Param #
=============================================================
modelo_keras_1 (InputLayer)      (None, 1)       0
_____________________________________________________________
camada_unica (Dense)             (None, 1)       2
_____________________________________________________________
link_logistic (Activation)       (None, 1)       0
=============================================================
Total params: 2
Trainable params: 2
Non-trainable params: 0
_____________________________________________________________
The hypothesis we built has 2 parameters. Looks right! \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\).
Now it’s the loss function’s turn.
Since our goal is to build a logistic regression, we’ll choose the binary_crossentropy loss function, which is a synonym for the logistic deviance, the more common term in the statistics world.
The 'accuracy' metric doesn’t go into the loss function optimizer; we use it to compare the models we create. Here we’ll compare against the glm model fitted above (but, for example, with rare events 'accuracy' won’t be very informative, so we could use 'auc', 'gini', etc.).

modelo_keras_1 %>% compile(
  loss = 'binary_crossentropy',
  optimizer = optimizer_sgd(lr = 0.4),
  metrics = c('accuracy')
)

modelo_keras_1_fit <- modelo_keras_1 %>% fit(
  x = df$x,
  y = df$y_1,
  epochs = 20,
  batch_size = 1000,
  verbose = 0
)


# coefficients
modelo_keras_1 %>% get_layer("camada_unica") %>% get_weights

# [[1]]
#          [,1]
# [1,] 2.000054
#
# [[2]]
# [1] -1.015561

# accuracy
loss_and_metrics_1 <- modelo_keras_1 %>% evaluate(df$x, df$y_1, batch = 100000, verbose = 0)
loss_and_metrics_1[[2]]

# [1] 0.85053

Identical results! It had to be so, because we built the same hypothesis and the same loss function as glm.


Logistic regression for \(Y_2\) (with glm)
To model \(Y_2\) we’ll step onto ground that linear models don’t tread. First I try to fit a curve using x and the transformation tanh(x). Let’s suppose I chose this predictor after a thorough and lengthy inspection of the data (I tried to simulate roughly what I would do in a modeling task where I’d have to build the features by hand).

# glm model 2 -------------------------------------------------------
modelo_glm_2 <- glm(y_2 ~ x + tanh(x), data = df, family = binomial)

# coefficients
coef(modelo_glm_2)

# (Intercept)           x     tanh(x)
#  -1.6698641   0.3043212   2.0936353

# accuracy
conf_matrix_glm_2 <- table(modelo_glm_2$fitted.values > 0.5, df$y_2)
sum(diag(conf_matrix_glm_2))/sum(conf_matrix_glm_2)

# [1] 0.82204

82% accuracy, not bad. But the hypothesis and parameters were different from the true data generator. Let’s use neural networks to solve the non-linearity problem.


Deep Learning for \(Y_2\) (with keras)
Hypothesis for \(E[Y_2|x]\).

# keras model 2 --------------------------------------------------------
input_keras_2 <- layer_input(1, name = "modelo_keras_2")

output_keras_2 <- input_keras_2 %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, name = "camada_um") %>%
  layer_activation("tanh", input_shape = 1, name = "tanh_de_dentro") %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, input_shape = 1, name = "camada_dois") %>%
  layer_activation("sigmoid", input_shape = 1, name = "link_logistic")

modelo_keras_2 <- keras_model(input_keras_2, output_keras_2)

summary(modelo_keras_2)

Model
_____________________________________________________________
Layer (type)                Output Shape           Param #
=============================================================
modelo_keras_2 (InputLayer) (None, 1)              0
_____________________________________________________________
camada_um (Dense)           (None, 1)              2
_____________________________________________________________
tanh_de_dentro (Activation) (None, 1)              0
_____________________________________________________________
camada_dois (Dense)         (None, 1)              2
_____________________________________________________________
link_logistic (Activation)  (None, 1)              0
=============================================================
Total params: 4.0
Trainable params: 4.0
Non-trainable params: 0.0
_____________________________________________________________

Four ‘trainable’ parameters, that’s it! Two parameters inside the tanh and the two parameters outside. We need keras to give us back -1, 2, -1 and 2, the way we generated the data.
Cost function

modelo_keras_2 %>% compile(
  loss = 'binary_crossentropy',
  optimizer = optimizer_sgd(lr = 0.1),
  metrics = c('accuracy')
)

modelo_keras_2_fit <- modelo_keras_2 %>% fit(
  x = df$x,
  y = df$y_2,
  epochs = 20,
  batch_size = 100,
  verbose = 0
)

# coefficients
modelo_keras_2 %>% get_layer("camada_um") %>% get_weights

# [[1]]
#          [,1]
# [1,] 2.012015
#
# [[2]]
# [1] -1.058052

modelo_keras_2 %>% get_layer("camada_dois") %>% get_weights

# [[1]]
#          [,1]
# [1,] 1.981977
#
# [[2]]
# [1] -1.006567

# accuracy
loss_and_metrics_2 <- modelo_keras_2 %>% evaluate(df$x, df$y_2, batch_size = 100000)
loss_and_metrics_2[[2]]

# [1] 0.82221

82% accuracy as well, but now the parameters are very close to the ones that generated the data! We just saw a set of parameters being found even with a non-linear relationship between them and the mean.
The accuracy of the two models ended up about the same, but the plot of the hypotheses found (below) shows that the glm curve is worse than the keras curve.

df %>%
  select(x, y_2) %>%
  mutate(x_cat = cut_number(x, n = 50)) %>%
  group_by(x_cat) %>%
  summarise(p = mean(y_2),
            x = mean(x),
            keras = logistic(-1.006567 + 1.981977 * tanh(-1.058052 + 2.012015 * x)),
            glm = logistic(-1.6698641 + 0.3043212*x + 2.0936353 * tanh(x)),
            n = n()) %>%
  mutate(logit_p = logit(p)) %>%
  gather(Modelo, estimativa, keras, glm) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = x_cat, y = p)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x_cat, y = estimativa, colour = Modelo, group = Modelo)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "x", colour = "resposta")










(Bonus) PCA with an autoencoder
In practice, PCA and autoencoders are used to reduce the dimensionality of the data. PCA is a particular case of an autoencoder with only one layer and linear activation functions. The post Construindo Autoencoders (in Portuguese) shows how to build one and I recommend reading it.
Summary: the autoencoder is an amazing technique that generalizes PCA.

title: Logistic Regression in: the world’s smallest deep learning
text:
Discussion
In my opinion, what happened is that a lot of old, well-established stuff had its name changed and was presented as new, and this ended up overshadowing the truly relevant contributions of research around neural networks and deep learning.
You can see that Deep Learning has generalized quite a lot, so I declare this post a success if what’s written above sparked curiosity to learn more about deep learning and add it to the work that was already being done. It’s more worthwhile to bring all statistics and machine learning practitioners together in this novelty than to divide ourselves.
I believe that, more than ever, theoretical foundations and interpretation will have their value boosted by the spread of deep learning. With the myth that deep learning is a panacea, and with how easy it has made building a predictive model, there’s a risk of being buried by black boxes made by people who neglect important aspects like interpretability, causality and generalization. Maybe bayesianism will emerge (once again) as the solution to qualitative problems in an increasingly obscure world, shedding light on the excesses of complex models and the benefits of simple ones.
Speaking of bayesianism (and inference in general), the results already obtained for linear models still apply to deep learning. And we also have the advantage that all the other tools used in deep learning that don’t affect the linearity of the parameters can be used, like convolutional, recurrent, max pooling, drop out, autoencoder and so many others.
To wrap up, in practice I suggest applying deep learning with Keras, an amazing package that uses tensorflow or theano behind the scenes. I believe you’ll see many posts about it here! (feel free to pester Dan Falbel, one of the partners of curso-r.com, who is involved in developing this R package =]).

title: Logistic Regression in: the world’s smallest deep learning
text:
Fun facts

N-th smallest deep learning
Above we saw the smallest and the second smallest Deep Learnings (which have nothing deep about them =P). But we can go as deep as we want! The neural network representation comes out easily:









The mathematical representation, on the other hand, gets weird:
\[E[Y|x] = \frac{1}{1 + \exp{\left(\beta_{p-1} + \beta_p\frac{1}{\frac{\vdots}{1 + \exp{\left(\beta_{6} + \beta_{7}\frac{1}{1 + \exp{\left(\beta_4 + \beta_5\frac{1}{1 + \exp{\left(\beta_2 + \beta_3\frac{1}{1 + \exp{\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1x\right)}}\right)}}\right)}}\right)}}}\right)}}\]


Vocabulary
Deep learning jargon and terms were inherited from a context different from the predictive modeling studied in statistics, and so countless synonyms came up. Some of them are:

activation function = link function
Softmax = multinomial likelihood
sigmoid = S-shaped function (in tensorflow the default is the logistic)
weights = parameters/betas/coefficients
binary crossentropy = deviance of the binomial distribution (logistic regression)

That’s it, we have to stay curious, ask questions and talk to each other. Cheers!

title: Principal Components: Intuition
text:
Principal components are widely used in statistical modeling, but their rigorous mathematical definition makes PCA look like a more abstract concept than we can grasp, especially when people say “maximize the total variance” and “reduce the dimensionality”. The first reaction is a big “HUH?”.
Below are some 3D plots that give a good illustration of what these two statements mean and, even though it’s a simple example, they’ll help extrapolate the idea to more complex problems.

title: Dropping highly correlated features can throw away the signal
text:
I’ve filtered out one feature of every pair with \(\text{cor}(X_i, X_k) > 0.97\) for most of my career. The reasoning: if two features are almost the same, keeping both adds nothing.
A while ago I posted on LinkedIn a simulation where that rule fails. When the signal lives in a ratio or a difference of two features, \(X_1/X_2\) or \(X_1 - X_2\), both features matter, even with \(\text{cor}(X_1, X_2) = 0.99\). This post walks through the simulation code.

title: Dropping highly correlated features can throw away the signal
text:
The data

library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(bonsai)
library(lightgbm)
library(patchwork)
library(corrr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
f <- glue::glue

add_dummy_feats <- function(df, n_new_feats) {
  n <- nrow(df)
  dummy_feats = replicate(n_new_feats, runif(n)) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    set_names(f("random{1:n_new_feats}"))
  df %>% bind_cols(dummy_feats)
}

Think of X_12m as some quantity measured over the last 12 months, and X_06m as the same quantity over the last 6 months. X_06m is X_12m minus a small random amount, so the two are almost identical. The target depends only on their ratio, X_06_12 = X_06m/X_12m. Three pure-noise features complete the data.

set.seed(123)
n = 100000
data <- tibble(
  X_12m = runif(n),
  X_06m = X_12m - pmin(X_12m, rgamma(n, 0.2, 55 - (X_12m + 1)*26)),
  X_06_12 = X_06m/X_12m,
  target = rbinom(n, 1, prob = 1/(1 + exp(-1 * (-60 + 60*X_06_12)))),
) %>% mutate(
  target = as.factor(if_else(target == 1, "a_1", "b_0"))
) %>%
  add_dummy_feats(3)

data %>%
  count(target) %>%
  mutate(p = scales::percent(n/sum(n)))
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   target     n p    
##   <fct>  <int> <chr>
## 1 a_1    32522 33%  
## 2 b_0    67478 67%


cor_feats <- data %>%
  sample_frac(0.1) %>%
  select(starts_with("X")) %>%
  correlate() %>%
  stretch() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = r), show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r,2)), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "royalblue", high = "darkred", mid = "white",
                       midpoint = 0, limit = c(-1, 1)) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "Pearson Correlation", x = NULL, y = NULL)

X_06m_X_12m <- data %>%
  sample_frac(0.1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = X_12m, y = X_06m)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1)

cor_feats + X_06m_X_12m








X_06m and X_12m are the textbook case for the correlation filter. The ratio X_06_12, the feature that actually drives the target, has a weak correlation with either of them.

title: Dropping highly correlated features can throw away the signal
text:
Two models
In the simulation the ratio isn’t available to the model: in real life you’d have to know to build it. Both recipes drop X_06_12. The second one also drops X_12m, as the correlation filter would.

set.seed(123)
data_split <- initial_split(data, strata = target)
train_data <- training(data_split)
test_data <- testing(data_split)

lgbm_model <- boost_tree(
  mode = "classification",
  trees = 100,
  tree_depth = 5,
  learn_rate = 0.01
) %>%
  set_engine("lightgbm")

# keeps both X_12m and X_06m
recipe1 <- recipe(target ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_rm(X_06_12) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

# drops X_12m, as the correlation filter would
recipe2 <- recipe(target ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  step_rm(X_12m) %>%
  step_rm(X_06_12) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

fitted_model1 <- workflow(recipe1, lgbm_model) %>% fit(data = train_data)
fitted_model2 <- workflow(recipe2, lgbm_model) %>% fit(data = train_data)

title: Dropping highly correlated features can throw away the signal
text:
Results

results1 <- bind_cols(test_data, predict(fitted_model1, new_data = test_data, type = "prob"))
results2 <- bind_cols(test_data, predict(fitted_model2, new_data = test_data, type = "prob"))

roc_auc1 <- roc_auc(results1, truth = target, .pred_a_1)
roc_auc2 <- roc_auc(results2, truth = target, .pred_a_1)

bind_rows(
  "both features" = roc_auc1,
  "X_12m dropped" = roc_auc2,
  .id = "model"
)
## # A tibble: 2 × 4
##   model         .metric .estimator .estimate
##   <chr>         <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
## 1 both features roc_auc binary         0.650
## 2 X_12m dropped roc_auc binary         0.543


roc_plot <- function(results, auc, title) {
  roc_curve(results, truth = target, .pred_a_1) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = 1 - specificity, y = sensitivity)) +
    geom_path(linewidth = 1) +
    geom_abline(lty = 3, linewidth = 1) +
    labs(title = title, x = "1 - Specificity", y = "Sensitivity") +
    annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 0.2, label = paste("AUC =", round(auc$.estimate, 2)),
             size = 8, color = "royalblue")
}

feat_imp_plot <- function(fitted_model) {
  lgb.importance(extract_fit_engine(fitted_model)) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Feature, Gain), y = Gain)) +
    geom_col() +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = "Feature importance", x = NULL, y = "Gain")
}

final_plot <- roc_plot(results1, roc_auc1, "ROC curve: both features") + feat_imp_plot(fitted_model1) +
  roc_plot(results2, roc_auc2, "ROC curve: X_12m dropped") + feat_imp_plot(fitted_model2) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 2)
final_plot








With both features, the trees can split on X_12m and X_06m together and approximate their ratio, and the two features rank at the top of the importance. Without X_12m, the model sees X_06m alone, and the information in the ratio is gone. The AUROC drops from 0.65 to 0.54.

title: Dropping highly correlated features can throw away the signal
text:
What to check instead
The correlation between two features tells you whether they carry the same values, not whether they carry the same information about the target. The rule works when the second feature is a noisy copy of the first. It fails when the signal is in how they differ.
Checking \(\text{cor}(X_1, f(X_1, X_2))\) for ratios, differences and the like helps, but only for the combinations you think of. A better question to ask is whether the model uses the feature at all, and how that compares to a feature that is pure noise.
That is the random probe idea. Add one or more random features, the probes, to the data, fit a model, and rank every feature by its importance. A probe can’t carry any information about the target, so its importance is the level a useless feature reaches by chance. Features that rank below the probes are candidates to drop. The method goes back to Stoppiglia, Dreyfus, Dubois and Oussar, Ranking a Random Feature for Variable and Feature Selection (JMLR, 2003), which also gives a statistical stopping rule for where to cut the ranking.



The random probe strategy: add noise features, fit a tree model, rank features by importance, and drop those below the best probe.


A random forest is a good model for the ranking: it captures interactions such as the ratio here without you having to build them, and its feature importance comes for free. Ready-made tools:

R: {Boruta} (Kursa and Rudnicki, Journal of Statistical Software, 2010) wraps a random forest. Its probes, the “shadow” features, are shuffled copies of each real feature. A feature is kept when its importance beats the best shadow more often than chance would allow, over many runs. Boruta looks for all relevant features, so it keeps redundant ones too: the opposite of the correlation filter.
Python: ProbeFeatureSelection from feature-engine adds random probe features, fits a scikit-learn model with cross-validation, and drops the features whose importance is below the probes’ (their mean, their maximum, or the mean plus 3 standard deviations).

The simulation already has probes: random1, random2 and random3. In the feature importance plot of the model with both features, X_12m and X_06m are far above all three, so the probe rule keeps both, which is what this data needs. The correlation filter would have dropped one of them.
The gist also has commented-out versions with the product, the difference and the sum in place of the ratio, if you want to try them.
Was this obvious to you? New? Or misleading in practice? I’d like to know.

title: Data Challenge - Image recovery
text:
Files with the .jpg extension store 5 coordinates, which are enough for the computer to understand and draw the image:

x and y: the cartesian coordinates of the image; and
r, g and b: red, green and blue, respectively, which together form colors.

Every color we know can be made by combining these three colors. The intensity of each color ranges from 0 to 1. For each point on the (x,y) plane there is an associated color. So an image can be represented by a dataset with 5 columns (x, y, r, g and b) whose number of rows is the number of pixels in the image.

Goals

Find out which model, linear regression or decision trees, is the most suitable to recover the blue component of the purple_wave.jpg image.



Find out which model, linear regression or decision trees, is the most suitable to recover the blue component of the xadrez_colorido.jpg image.




How to start?
With the help of the readJPEG() function from the jpeg package, load one of the images into R and turn it into a data.frame:

library(tidyverse)
library(jpeg)
# loads a jpeg image into R
download.file("http://curso-r.comimages/posts/conteudo/desafio-recuperacao-img/purple_wave.webp", 
              destfile = "purple_wave.jpg")

img <- readJPEG("purple_wave.jpg")

# turns the image array into a data.frame with position (x,y)
# and color (r,g,b) info; image dimensions
img_dim <- dim(img)

# RGB to data.frame
img_df <- data.frame(
  x = rep(1:img_dim[2], each = img_dim[1]),
  y = rep(img_dim[1]:1, img_dim[2]),
  r = as.vector(img[,,1]),
  g = as.vector(img[,,2]),
  b = as.vector(img[,,3])
) %>%
  mutate(cor = rgb(r, g, b),
         id = 1:n())

Split the data.frame into two parts: one with the blue (column b) and one without. - Part 1) x, y, r, g - Part 2) x, y, r, g, b

# for reproducibility
set.seed(2018) 
# Part 1) x, y, r, g
img_df_parte1 <- img_df %>% 
  sample_frac(3/5) %>% # taking 3/5 of the dataset
  mutate(b_backup = b, # backup of the original blue
         b = 0, # removing the blue from the image
         cor = rgb(r, g, b)) # image color without the blue
# Part 2) x, y, r, g, b
img_df_parte2 <- img_df %>% filter(!id%in%img_df_parte1$id)

Visualizing:

# Image without the blue
ggplot(data = img_df_parte1, aes(x = x, y = y)) + 
  geom_point(colour = img_df_parte1$cor) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y", title = "Imagem sem B (azul)") +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
  theme_bw()








Your task is to recover the blue (which we erased from the image) in Part 1, using predictive models built with Part 2 (which still has the blue!) for both images (xadrez_colorido and purple_wave).


Result
The result of this data challenge will be published on the blog on August 24! Good luck!

title: Gentle introduction to the learning rate parameter
text:
I found an old gist on my GitHub about the learning rate. It fits a regression line by gradient descent, and it’s oddly satisfying to watch. A bit insightful too.
There are three curves, one for each learning rate:

title: Gentle introduction to the learning rate parameter
text:
The learning rate
Gradient descent updates the model parameters a little at each step, in the direction that lowers the loss:
\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, \nabla L(\theta_t)\]
The learning rate \(\eta\) is the size of that step. The optimizer below is Adam, which adapts the step for each parameter, but the learning rate still sets its scale.

title: Gentle introduction to the learning rate parameter
text:
The code
The data is the cars dataset: stopping distance (dist) as a function of speed. The model is dist ~ speed + speed^2, written as a linear layer with two inputs.

library(torch)
torch_manual_seed(1)

x <- torch_tensor(cbind(cars$speed, cars$speed^2))
y <- torch_tensor(cars$dist)$unsqueeze(2)
mse <- nn_mse_loss()

model_gen <- function(lr) {
  lin <- nn_linear(2, 1)  # b0, b1 and b2
  opt <- torch::optim_adam(lin$parameters, lr = lr)
  return(list(lin = lin, opt = opt))
}

model_fit <- function(model) {
  model$opt$zero_grad()

  pred <- model$lin(x) # b0 + b1*speed + b2*speed^2
  custo <- mse(y, pred)
  custo$backward()
  model$opt$step()
  return(pred)
}

Three copies of the same model, one per learning rate:

model1 <- model_gen(2)
model2 <- model_gen(0.05)
model3 <- model_gen(0.001)

Each iteration takes one optimizer step for each model and draws the three fitted curves. The original gist plots to the screen with Sys.sleep(0.1) between steps. Here gifski::save_gif() records each plot as a frame instead.

gifski::save_gif({
  for (i in 1:100) {
    pred1 <- model_fit(model1)
    pred2 <- model_fit(model2)
    pred3 <- model_fit(model3)
    plot(cars, main = paste("step", i))
    lines(x[, 1]$unsqueeze(2), pred1, col = "red", lwd = 4)
    lines(x[, 1]$unsqueeze(2), pred2, col = "royalblue", lwd = 4)
    lines(x[, 1]$unsqueeze(2), pred3, col = "orange", lwd = 4)
  }
}, gif_file = "learning_rate.gif", width = 640, height = 480, delay = 0.1)

Tune your models, folks!

title: Winding a cosine around a circle: the Fourier transform in a GIF
text: A while ago I posted on LinkedIn an #rstats GIF inspired by 3Blue1Brown’s But what is the Fourier Transform? A visual introduction. This post is that GIF, with the code behind it.

title: Winding a cosine around a circle: the Fourier transform in a GIF
text:
The idea
Take a signal \(g(t)\), here \(g(t) = \cos(20t)\) for \(t\) between 0 and 1, and wrap it around the origin of the complex plane. Each point of the signal becomes \(g(t)\,e^{i\omega t}\): the angle comes from \(t\) and the winding frequency \(\omega\), and the distance from the origin comes from \(g(t)\).
Then take the centre of mass of the wrapped curve, the average of all its points:
\[
\hat{g}(\omega) = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T g(t)\,e^{i\omega t}\,dt
\]

left panel: the wrapped curve for the current \(\omega\) and its centre of mass (red dot).
right panel: the real part of the centre of mass as \(\omega\) goes from 0.4 to 40.

For most winding frequencies the curve spreads evenly around the origin and the centre of mass stays near 0. When \(\omega = 20\), the frequency of the cosine, the peaks of the signal all land on the same side of the circle and the centre of mass jumps to about 0.5. That spike is the frequency showing up in the Fourier transform.

title: Winding a cosine around a circle: the Fourier transform in a GIF
text:
The code
f() is the signal and expi() is \(e^{ix}\) written as \(\cos x + i \sin x\). For each a, x runs from 0 to a * L and the signal is evaluated at x / (a * L), which goes from 0 to 1. So expi(x) * f(x / (a * L)) is \(g(t)\,e^{i\omega t}\) with \(\omega = a L\).

f <- function(x) cos(x*20)
expi <- function(x) cos(x) + sin(x)*1i
L <- 40
medias_Re <- c()
fs <- c()
as <- seq(0.01, 1, l = 140)

The original gist writes the GIF with animation::saveGIF(), which needs ImageMagick, and pauses with Sys.sleep(0.1) between frames. Here gifski::save_gif() records each plot as a frame instead, so par(mfrow = c(1,2)) moves inside the block to apply to the GIF’s device.

gifski::save_gif({
  par(mfrow = c(1,2))
  for(a in as) {
    x <- seq(0, a*40, l = 500)
    ft <- expi(x)*f(x/(a*L))
    media_Re <- mean(Re(ft))
    plot(Re(ft), Im(ft), xlim = c(-1.2, 1.2), ylim = c(-1.2, 1.2), main = "cos(20t) - Mass Center on Complex Plane")
    points(media_Re, mean(Im(ft)), col = "red", cex = 3, pch = 16 )
    medias_Re <- c(medias_Re, media_Re)
    fs <- c(fs, a*L)
    plot(fs, medias_Re, type = "l", xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(-0.11, 0.51))
    points(a*L, media_Re, col = "red", cex = 3, pch = 16)
  }
}, gif_file = "fourier.gif", width = 600, height = 300, delay = 0.1)

The video goes further, from this centre-of-mass picture to the Fourier transform formula itself.

title: Lollapalooza according to Spotify
text:
On the day I went to Lollapalooza I discovered Rspotify, a wrapper for the Spotify API, and that gave me the idea of putting together info from both.
The fun here will involve
This year’s Lollapalooza in São Paulo had 47 bands spread over four stages. The fun part is linking the Lolla schedule to the band popularity info provided by Spotify. Below I describe how I got the data, list the three hypotheses I came up with and make some plots to discuss them.

title: Lollapalooza according to Spotify
text:
Dataset

Prerequisites
Packages

# installs Rspotify
if(!require("Rspotify"))
  devtools::install_github("tiagomendesdantas/Rspotify")


library(Rspotify)
library(magrittr)
library(forcats)
library(stringi)
library(lubridate)
library(httr)
library(rvest)
library(tidyverse)

Rspotify is a new package that isn’t on CRAN yet, but it already works.
Spotify account
To use the Spotify API you need an account on their website, as you can imagine.
Spotify App
To get an access code for their API you need to create an App within your Spotify account; this is the most bureaucratic prerequisite of all. I learned how to do it by following the steps in the README of the Rspotify package itself on Github (see here).
In the end, you’ll have an app_id, a client_id and a client_secret in hand.


Extracting the Lollapalooza SP 2017 schedule
The goal here is to get a data.frame version of the tables on the website lollapaloozabr.com/lineup-horarios/. It has the full schedule for both days of the event.
On to the code! Tip: the best way to learn what each step of the code does is to run it line by line and look at the result.

# schedule from the lollapalooza 2017 website ------------------

lolla2017_programacao <- "https://www.lollapaloozabr.com/lineup-horarios/" %>%
  GET() %>%
  read_html() %>%
  html_table() %>%
  set_names(c("sabado", "domingo")) %>%
  at_depth(2, ~ .x %>%
             stri_replace_all_regex(" {2,}", "") %>%
             stri_replace_all_regex("[\\n]{1}", ",") %>%
             stri_replace_all_regex("[,]{2,}", "\\\n") %>%
             read.csv(text = ., header = FALSE,
                      col.names = c("artist", "hora"))) %>%
  map(~ .x[-1] %>%
        data_frame(palco = names(.), programacao_palco = .) %>%
        unnest(programacao_palco)) %>%
  data_frame(dia = names(.), programacao = .) %>%
  unnest(programacao) %>%
  separate(hora, c("hora_ini", "hora_fim"), sep = "-") %>%
  mutate(artist = artist %>% tolower,
         hora_ini = paste(if_else(dia %in% "sabado", "2017-03-25", "2017-03-26"), hora_ini) %>% ymd_hm(),
         hora_ini = if_else(hour(hora_ini) < 12, hora_ini + hours(12), hora_ini),
         hora_fim = paste(if_else(dia %in% "sabado", "2017-03-25", "2017-03-26"), hora_fim) %>% ymd_hm(),
         hora_fim = if_else(hour(hora_fim) < 12, hora_fim + hours(12), hora_fim),
         dia = fct_relevel(dia, c("sabado", "domingo")))

Extracting the popularity of the Lollapalooza bands on Spotify
Now let’s use the Rspotify package to extract the popularity of the bands listed in the lolla2017_programacao data.frame. For that, I used an official Spotify playlist made by the Lollapalooza team itself. This playlist is identified by the id 1mHoPn6JpbtWtoBuvSXrVm in the Spotify database.

  data_frame(artist = .) %>%

         artist_info = map2(search_artist, artist, ~ {
           if(.x %>% is.na) {data.frame(search_artist = NA)} else {
           .x %>%
             mutate(name = name %>% tolower) %>%
             filter(name %in% .y) %>%
             head(1)

  unnest(artist_info) %>%

title: Lollapalooza according to Spotify
text:
Results

Hypothesis I

Hypothesis I: the organizers used the strategy of spreading band popularity evenly throughout the day.

One of the many logistical challenges of the event is allocating the bands to time slots across the four different stages.
I went to the event on Saturday and heard that Cage The Elephant had been one of the first bands to play. I knew how popular the band was (according to Spotify, more popular than The Strokes) and right away I found it odd that the event had them play so early.

lolla2017_grafico <- lolla2017 %>%
  mutate(hora = map2(hora_ini, hora_fim, ~ seq(.x, .y, 30*60) %>% floor_date("30 minutes"))) %>%
  unnest(hora) %>%
  group_by(dia, hora, palco) %>%
  summarise(artist = first(artist),
            n = n(),
            mean_popularity = mean(popularity))

lolla2017_grafico %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ymd_hm(format(hora, "2017-03-26 %H%M")), y = mean_popularity, colour = palco)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = lolla2017_grafico %>% filter(artist %in% "cage the elephant"), colour = "red", size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = lolla2017_grafico %>% filter(artist %in% "cage the elephant") %>% head(1), aes(label = artist), colour = "red", hjust = 0, vjust = -1) +
  facet_wrap(~dia) +
  labs(x = "Hora do dia", y = "Popularidade média") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16))








The plot above agrees with the common sense that the popular ones are left for the end, which doesn’t help confirm the hypothesis that Cage The Elefant was badly placed.


Hypothesis II

Hypothesis II: in terms of band popularity, Sunday was better than Saturday.

Talking with friends and acquaintances, I noticed that most of them were either going on Sunday or would rather go on Sunday if they had the chance. This made me wonder whether there really was a higher concentration of good bands on Sunday.

ggplot(lolla2017 %>%
         mutate(artist = artist %>% fct_reorder(popularity, .desc = TRUE))) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = artist, y = popularity, fill = dia), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.4))









ggplot(lolla2017) +
 geom_density(aes(fill = dia, x = popularity, colour = dia), fill = NA) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.4))








Conclusion: nothing suggests there was an imbalance. I think my circle of friends has some strange bias.


Hypothesis III

Hypothesis III: band popularity was balanced across the different stages.

When I questioned hypothesis I, I also thought about how hard it is to place the bands on the different stages. Since thousands of people would be fighting for space, it would be in the organizers’ interest to keep them as spread out as possible for several reasons: better queue flow, more comfort, less risk of accidents, among others, and a good way to do that would be to make the stages equally attractive so there wouldn’t be a big crowd in a single spot.

ggplot(lolla2017 %>%
         mutate(palco = palco %>% as.factor %>% fct_reorder(popularity, mean))) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = palco, y = popularity, x = 1)) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.text.x = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "")








The Skol stage had the least variation in popularity and usually had artists of medium to high popularity, but the AXE and Onix stages got the heavyweight artists. The Perry’s stage hosted the most lesser-known artists.

title: Lollapalooza according to Spotify
text:
Final remarks
The topic covered here wasn’t useful, I agree, but we went through almost every step of a typical data analysis process. We did web scraping, used APIs, tidied the data, structured the information, created variables and made plots. Only the modeling part was left out. And it’s no coincidence that all the tidyverse packages were useful in this work.
The homework is to find some interesting data on the internet and apply the steps we learned here!

title: Are tree-based models immune to multicollinearity?
text:
Tree-based models like decision trees, random forest, ligthGBM and xgboost are known, among other qualities, for their robustness to multicollinearity. It’s well known that their predictive power isn’t shaken by the presence of extremely correlated variables.
But who has never used a Random Forest for variable selection? Taking, for example, the top 10 most important ones and dropping the rest?
Or even ventured an interpretation and drew conclusions from the order of the most important variables?
Below we show why we shouldn’t ignore multicollinearity completely!

title: Are tree-based models immune to multicollinearity?
text:
A nice little model
First let’s fit a nice little model, free of multicollinearity. Suppose we want to predict Petal.Length using the sepal measurements (Sepal.Width and Sepal.Length) from our good old iris dataset.

library(tidyverse)

iris2 <- iris %>% select(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, Petal.Length)
iris2 %>% cor %>% corrplot::corrplot()








The plot above shows that the explanatory variables are not strongly correlated. Fitting a random fores, we get the following variable importance order:

library(randomForest)
iris2_rf <- randomForest(Petal.Length ~ ., data = iris2)
varImpPlot(iris2_rf)








No surprises. Now on to the problem!

title: Are tree-based models immune to multicollinearity?
text:
An ugly model
Let’s forge an extreme situation where many variables are multicollinear. I’ll do this by repeating the Sepal.Length column several times.

iris3 <- accumulate(1:20, ~{
  .x[[paste0("Sepal.Length", .y)]] <-  iris2$Sepal.Length
  .x
}, .init = iris2)

iris3[[20]] %>% cor %>% corrplot::corrplot(order = "alphabet")








Now things are ugly! We have 20 perfectly collinear variables. Even so, a random forest on this new dataset wouldn’t lose predictive power.
But what happened to the variable importance?

iris3_rf <- randomForest(Petal.Length ~ ., data = iris3[[20]])
varImpPlot(iris3_rf)








Here the tables have turned: we would conclude that Sepal.Width is the most important of all the variables!

title: Are tree-based models immune to multicollinearity?
text:
Flawed variable selection
The plot below shows that the more correlated variables we have, the lower the importance of ALL OF THEM AT THE SAME TIME! It’s as if the collinear variables split the importance among themselves.

# fits a random forest on datasets with 1 to 20 repetitions of `Sepal.Length`
rfs <- map(iris3, ~ randomForest(Petal.Length ~ ., data = .x) %>% importance)

# extracts the importances of the `Sepal.Length` repetitions
importancia <- map_dfr(rfs, ~{
  .x %>% 
    as.data.frame() %>% 
    tibble::rownames_to_column() %>% 
    dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(rowname, "^Sepal.Length"))
}, .id = "n_repeticoes") %>%
  mutate(n_repeticoes = as.numeric(n_repeticoes))

# Plot of the number of multicollinear variables vs importance
importancia %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_repeticoes, y = IncNodePurity)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 40, size = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Qtd de repetições da coluna `Sepal.Length`", y = "Importância", title = "Gráfico da relação entre o número de variáveis multicolineares vs importância")








In practice, if we set an importance cutoff to drop variables (as illustrated by the red line), we would have a potential problem: we could be throwing away very important information.

title: Are tree-based models immune to multicollinearity?
section: So how do we deal with multicollinearity?
text:
So how do we deal with multicollinearity?
Some ways to deal with multicollinearity are:

Looking at the correlation matrix
VIF
Recursive feature elimination

title: Are tree-based models immune to multicollinearity?
text:
Conclusion
Be careful when throwing everything into the pot! We should always worry about multicollinearity, even when fitting tree-based models.
Cheers!

remotes::install_github("Athospd/targetsboard")

library(targetsboard)

title: Bechdel: Movies and Sexism
text:
A friend introduced me to the Bechdel Test (in Portuguese), which checks whether a movie meets three basic rules:
The test was named after the cartoonist Alison Bechdel (in Portuguese), who presented this idea in one of her comic strips, and today it is used to measure the degree of gender discrimination in film.
The website bechdeltest.com lets anyone contribute movies rated on the Bechdel test and provides easy access to a database of 8,440 movies from 1888 to the present day.
A personal two cents (Athos): Imagine the same rules, but swapping man for woman. How many movies do you think would fail the test? My opinion? Less than 1%!

title: Bechdel: Movies and Sexism

text:
Rating
The rating goes from 0 to 3 and represents how many rules the movie meets. Let’s label it for easier reading.

bechdel <- bechdel %>%
  mutate(
    indice_bechdel = case_when(
      rating == 0 ~ "Menos de duas mulheres",
      rating == 1 ~ "Pelo menos duas mulheres",
      rating == 2 ~ "... que conversam entre si",
      rating == 3 ~ "... sobre algo que não seja homem"
    ),
    indice_bechdel = fct_reorder(indice_bechdel, rating),
    decada = (year %/% 10)*10
  )


bechdel %>% 
  count(indice_bechdel, rating) %>%
  mutate(
    rating_p = scales::percent(n/sum(n), accuracy = 1)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = indice_bechdel, x = n)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = 0, yend = indice_bechdel)) +
  geom_point(size = 12) +
  geom_text(aes(label = rating_p), color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(x = "contagem", y = NULL, title = "Filmes por Rating Bechdel") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )

title: Bechdel: Movies and Sexism
text:
Evolution over the Decades

bechdel_por_decada <- bechdel %>%
  count(decada, indice_bechdel, .drop = FALSE)

bechdel_por_decada %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = decada, fill = indice_bechdel, y = n)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill", colour = "black", width = 10) +
  geom_text(aes(label = indice_bechdel), position = "fill", data = filter(bechdel_por_decada, decada == 1950), vjust = 2.5, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Década", y = "Proporção", title = "Evolução dos Ratings Bechdel pelas Décadas") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) 








Bechdel Test results have been improving over time, so the outlook is positive. In an increasingly connected world, the hope is that information reaches more and more people and the discrimination ingrained in our culture dissolves.

title: Bechdel: Movies and Sexism
text:
IMDB information
The IMDB API is very bureaucratic to use. I found the OMDB website, which was much easier to use, though it may have less cool information. Here’s how to use it:

API Key
First I got an API KEY on their website and put it in my .Renviron, because then I can use Sys.get() to use it without having to show it to anyone.

Sys.getenv('OMDB_APIKEY')
# [1] as48732f1d (just pretend)



Calling the API
Then I called the OMDB API using both my API KEY and the IMDB ID. The call has to look like this: http://www.omdbapi.com/?apikey={Sys.getenv('OMDB_APIKEY')}&i=tt{imdbid}. It returns a json that can be easily formatted with jsonlite::fromJSON().

library(glue)
pega_info_imdb <- function(imdbid) {
  glue("http://www.omdbapi.com/?apikey={Sys.getenv('OMDB_APIKEY')}&i=tt{imdbid}") %>%
    fromJSON() %>%
    as_tibble()
}
# safely because the API may return error 522 (on the OMDB server)
pega_info_imdb_safe <- safely(pega_info_imdb)

# takes ~40 min
bechdel_com_imdb <- bechdel %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(
    infos_imdb = map(imdbid, pega_info_imdb_safe)
  )



Tidying the data
The data needs some massaging first because it comes as a nested list, all as text.

# Tidies the nested tables
arruma_infos_imdb <- function(infos_imdb) {
  if(!is.null(infos_imdb$Ratings)) {
    infos_imdb %>% 
      nest(Ratings = c(Ratings)) %>%
      mutate(Ratings = map(Ratings, ~.x$Ratings %>% filter(Source %in% "Internet Movie Database"))) %>%
      unnest(Ratings)
  } else {
    infos_imdb
  }
}

# creates bechdel with the imdb info and fixes the variable types
bechdel_com_imdb <- bechdel_com_imdb %>%
  mutate(
    deu_errado = map_lgl(infos_imdb, ~ !is.null(.x$error)),
    infos_imdb = infos_imdb %>% map("result") %>% map(arruma_infos_imdb)
  ) %>%
  unnest(infos_imdb) %>%
  mutate(
    imdbRating_num = imdbRating %>% parse_number()

title: How to make R tell you on telegram that bitcoin is cheap
text:
The highlight of the story is R sending a message to Telegram. Just to get you motivated, I’ll tell you about something fun I did with telegram and bitcoin prices.
Hero of the day: Luca Biglia, author of the R telegram package.

title: How to make R tell you on telegram that bitcoin is cheap
text:
Ingredients
For today’s craft project we’ll need:

A telegram bot
The R package library(telegram)
The BlinkTrade API
String and a tube of glue

The steps we need to follow to get there are:

Create an .Rproj (RStudio project).
install and load the R telegram package.
Create a telegram bot with the help of BotFather.
Connect R to the bot.
Query and store bitcoin prices every 30 seconds.
create an infinite loop in R to track the prices nonstop.
Make R send us a message when the price of bitcoin is above X, for example.
(extra) Come up with wild ideas of what to do with telegram + R.

title: How to make R tell you on telegram that bitcoin is cheap
text:
Introduction to the components
First of all, a brief introduction to the things that will show up here:

telegram: just like Whatsapp, but better.
BotFather: a contact on your phone (on telegram) that helps you create a telegram bot.
bitcoin: a successful digital currency.
BlinkTrade: among other things, provides an API for real-time bitcoin values.

title: How to make R tell you on telegram that bitcoin is cheap
text:
Bitcoin tracker
Go ahead and create your .Rproj, run install.packages("telegram");library(telegram) and let’s go straight to the third step.

Step 3: Telegram bot - Create a bot
A bot is like one more person in your telegram contact list, except they are machines instead of humans and respond to specific commands. The fun part is that you can customize these commands any way you like! You just need a purpose and to know how to program it.
The README on the package’s github is very good! I’ll summarize what’s there with small changes:

Go to your telegram and search for BotFather as if you were looking for a person in your contact list. Start a chat with him!
Send the text “/start” and then “/newbot”. Give your bot a name (it can be a cute name) and then a username for your bot, which must end in bot.
Now copy the token BotFather sent you and paste it into .Renviron. My bot has the username AthosDamianiBot, so I should name the variable like this:










If you use this naming convention you can use the bot_token() function to get your token. Otherwise you’ll have to resort to Sys.getenv().
NOTE: Restart R so that .Renviron takes effect.


Step 4: Telegram bot - Connect to R

Load the package and create a TGBot object for the bot you created earlier:


library(telegram)

bot <- TGBot$new(token = bot_token('AthosDamianiBot'))

bot$getMe()


Now we need the chat_id. To get it, search for your bot on telegram as if it were a contact (just like you did with BotFather) and start a chat with it.
In R, call the bot$getUpdates() method to get the messages you sent it into R and, finally, find the chat_id hidden in msgs.


msgs <- bot$getUpdates()

msgs$message$chat$id[1]

[1] 135717340


With the chat_id in hand, set it as the default chat_id.


bot$set_default_chat_id(135717340)

At this point we’re ready to interact with our bot!


Step 5: Query bitcoin prices
Bitcoin prices are provided by the BlinkTrade API, which is very simple to use: just grab the json that the url in the code below returns. While I’m at it, I give it a little polish to make it a data.frame with the query date attached.

library(jsonlite)
library(tidyverse)

safe_fromJSON <- safely(fromJSON, as.numeric(NA))
nova_consulta_list <- safe_fromJSON("https://api.blinktrade.com/api/v1/BRL/ticker?crypto_currency=BTC")

nova_consulta <- nova_consulta_list$result %>%
        as.tibble %>%
        mutate(timestamp = lubridate::now())

nova_consulta
# A tibble: 1 x 9
      high      vol      buy  last      low   pair  sell vol_brl           timestamp
     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>  <chr> <dbl>   <dbl>              <dttm>
1 14438.21 511.5911 14077.01 14200 13801.04 BTCBRL 14200 7257317 2017-08-18 17:09:44

NOTE: I used the safely() adverb because the API can choke at any moment, which would make R return an error that would stop the price tracking.


Step 6: Infinite loop to track the prices
The skeleton of the tracker is made of an infinite loop (while(TRUE)), a historico.RData data.frame, a wait time between one query and the next (30 seconds by default) and the query itself.

# initializes historico.RData
# historico <- nova_consulta
# save(historico, file = "historico.RData")

acompanhar_bitcoin <- function(frequencia = 30) {
  load("historico.RData")

  # infinite loop
  while(TRUE) {
    # gets the brazilian bitcoin quote (BTCBRL) from the blinktrade API
    nova_consulta_list <- safe_fromJSON("https://api.blinktrade.com/api/v1/BRL/ticker?crypto_currency=BTC")

    # checks whether the API returned a list
    if("list" %in% class(nova_consulta_list$result)) {
      nova_consulta <- nova_consulta_list$result %>%
        as.tibble %>%
        mutate(timestamp = lubridate::now())

      # ---------------------
      #
      # space reserved for the rules!
      #
      # ---------------------

      # stores the query
      historico <- bind_rows(historico, nova_consulta)
      save(historico, file = "historico.RData")
    }
  }
  Sys.sleep(frequencia)
}



Step 7: Rules for telegram messages
Now it’s time to decide what the bot should warn us about! I left two simple examples below using the bot$sendMessage() method, which, as the name suggests, makes the bot send us a message. Now, every time the price of bitcoin is below R$13,600 or above R$14,600 I’ll know right away!

# if the quote value meets some criterion, sends a message via telegram.
if(nova_consulta$buy < 13600 & nova_consulta$last > 13900) {
  bot$sendMessage('baixa!')
  bot$sendMessage(nova_consulta$buy)
}

# ...

if(nova_consulta$buy > 14600 & nova_consulta$last < 14500) {
  bot$sendMessage('alta!')
  bot$sendMessage(nova_consulta$buy)
}



Extra Step: Wild ideas of what to do with telegram + R
Creativity rules here. You can send plots, sounds, stickers and any kind of media. I made a ggplot to keep an eye on the trend, so I could ask my bot to show me the plot at any time.

# ... this goes inside the acompanhar_bitcoin() function
p <- ggplot(historico %>%
              gather(indicador, valor, high, low, buy, sell, last)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = timestamp, y = valor, colour = indicador))
print(p)

You can also program commands to pass to the Bot so it builds something for us, for example, you could create a command to buy or sell bitcoins in real time!
Julio once created a bot that was practically R itself: you sent code as a message and it returned R’s output! Later I’ll ask him to post something about it.
Anyway, there’s room to be clever here. All it takes is that brilliant shower idea.
Homework: - Send the “gemidão do zap” (a Brazilian prank audio) to 3 friends with a line of code.
cheers!

title: Simple audio classification with torch
text:
First published on the RStudio AI Blog on February 4, 2021.
This article translates Daniel Falbel’s ‘Simple Audio Classification’ article from tensorflow/keras to torch/torchaudio. The main goal is to introduce torchaudio and illustrate its contributions to the torch ecosystem. Here, we focus on a popular dataset, the audio loader and the spectrogram transformer. An interesting side product is the parallel between torch and tensorflow, showing sometimes the differences, sometimes the similarities between them.
library(torch)
library(torchaudio)

title: Simple audio classification with torch
text:
Downloading and Importing
torchaudio has the speechcommand_dataset built in. It filters out background_noise by default and lets us choose between versions v0.01 and v0.02.

# set an existing folder here to cache the dataset

title: Simple audio classification with torch
text:
Generator Dataloader
torch::dataloader has the same task as data_generator defined in the original article. It is responsible for preparing batches - including shuffling, padding, one-hot encoding, etc. - and for taking care of parallelism / device I/O orchestration.
In torch we do this by passing the train/test subset to torch::dataloader and encapsulating all the batch setup logic inside a collate_fn() function.

set.seed(6)
id_train <- sample(length(df), size = 0.7*length(df))
id_test <- setdiff(seq_len(length(df)), id_train)
# subsets

train_subset <- torch::dataset_subset(df, id_train)
test_subset <- torch::dataset_subset(df, id_test)

At this point, dataloader(train_subset) would not work because the samples are not padded. So we need to build our own collate_fn() with the padding strategy.
I suggest using the following approach when implementing the collate_fn():

begin with collate_fn <- function(batch) browser().
instantiate dataloader with the collate_fn()
create an environment by calling enumerate(dataloader) so you can ask to retrieve a batch from dataloader.
run environment[[1]][[1]]. Now you should be sent inside collate_fn() with access to batch input object.
build the logic.


collate_fn <- function(batch) {
  browser()
}

ds_train <- dataloader(
  train_subset, 
  batch_size = 32, 
  shuffle = TRUE, 
  collate_fn = collate_fn
)

ds_train_env <- enumerate(ds_train)
ds_train_env[[1]][[1]]

The final collate_fn() pads the waveform to length 16001 and then stacks everything up together. At this point there are no spectrograms yet. We going to make spectrogram transformation a part of model architecture.

pad_sequence <- function(batch) {
    # Make all tensors in a batch the same length by padding with zeros
    batch <- sapply(batch, function(x) (x$t()))
    batch <- torch::nn_utils_rnn_pad_sequence(batch, batch_first = TRUE, padding_value = 0.)
    return(batch$permute(c(1, 3, 2)))
  }

# Final collate_fn
collate_fn <- function(batch) {
 # Input structure:
 # list of 32 lists: list(waveform, sample_rate, label, speaker_id, utterance_number)
 # Transpose it
 batch <- purrr::transpose(batch)
 tensors <- batch$waveform
 targets <- batch$label_index

 # Group the list of tensors into a batched tensor
 tensors <- pad_sequence(tensors)
 
 # target encoding
 targets <- torch::torch_stack(targets)

 list(tensors = tensors, targets = targets) # (64, 1, 16001)
}

Batch structure is:

batch[[1]]: waveforms - tensor with dimension (32, 1, 16001)
batch[[2]]: targets - tensor with dimension (32, 1)

Also, torchaudio comes with 3 loaders, av_loader, tuner_loader, and audiofile_loader- more to come. set_audio_backend() is used to set one of them as the audio loader. Their performances differ based on audio format (mp3 or wav). There is no perfect world yet: tuner_loader is best for mp3, audiofile_loader is best for wav, but neither of them has the option of partially loading a sample from an audio file without bringing all the data into memory first.
For a given audio backend we need pass it to each worker through worker_init_fn() argument.

ds_train <- dataloader(
  train_subset, 
  batch_size = 128, 
  shuffle = TRUE, 
  collate_fn = collate_fn,
  num_workers = 16,
  worker_init_fn = function(.) {torchaudio::set_audio_backend("audiofile_loader")},
  worker_globals = c("pad_sequence") # pad_sequence is needed for collect_fn
)

ds_test <- dataloader(
  test_subset, 
  batch_size = 64, 
  shuffle = FALSE, 
  collate_fn = collate_fn,
  num_workers = 8,
  worker_globals = c("pad_sequence") # pad_sequence is needed for collect_fn
)

title: Simple audio classification with torch
text:
Model definition
Instead of keras::keras_model_sequential(), we are going to define a torch::nn_module(). As referenced by the original article, the model is based on this architecture for MNIST from this tutorial, and I’ll call it ‘DanielNN’.

dan_nn <- torch::nn_module(
  "DanielNN",
  
  initialize = function(
    window_size_ms = 30, 
    window_stride_ms = 10
  ) {
    
    # spectrogram spec
    window_size <- as.integer(16000*window_size_ms/1000)
    stride <- as.integer(16000*window_stride_ms/1000)
    fft_size <- as.integer(2^trunc(log(window_size, 2) + 1))
    n_chunks <- length(seq(0, 16000, stride))
    
    self$spectrogram <- torchaudio::transform_spectrogram(
      n_fft = fft_size, 
      win_length = window_size, 
      hop_length = stride, 
      normalized = TRUE, 
      power = 2
    )
    
    # convs 2D
    self$conv1 <- torch::nn_conv2d(in_channels = 1, out_channels = 32, kernel_size = c(3,3))
    self$conv2 <- torch::nn_conv2d(in_channels = 32, out_channels = 64, kernel_size = c(3,3))
    self$conv3 <- torch::nn_conv2d(in_channels = 64, out_channels = 128, kernel_size = c(3,3))
    self$conv4 <- torch::nn_conv2d(in_channels = 128, out_channels = 256, kernel_size = c(3,3))
    
    # denses
    self$dense1 <- torch::nn_linear(in_features = 14336, out_features = 128)
    self$dense2 <- torch::nn_linear(in_features = 128, out_features = 30)
  },
  
  forward = function(x) {
    x %>% # (64, 1, 16001)
      self$spectrogram() %>% # (64, 1, 257, 101)
      torch::torch_add(0.01) %>%
      torch::torch_log() %>%
      self$conv1() %>%
      torch::nnf_relu() %>%
      torch::nnf_max_pool2d(kernel_size = c(2,2)) %>%
      
      self$conv2() %>%
      torch::nnf_relu() %>%
      torch::nnf_max_pool2d(kernel_size = c(2,2)) %>%
      
      self$conv3() %>%
      torch::nnf_relu() %>%
      torch::nnf_max_pool2d(kernel_size = c(2,2)) %>%
      
      self$conv4() %>%
      torch::nnf_relu() %>%
      torch::nnf_max_pool2d(kernel_size = c(2,2)) %>%
      
      torch::nnf_dropout(p = 0.25) %>%
      torch::torch_flatten(start_dim = 2) %>%
      
      self$dense1() %>%
      torch::nnf_relu() %>%
      torch::nnf_dropout(p = 0.5) %>%
      self$dense2() 
  }
)

model <- dan_nn()


device <- torch::torch_device(if(torch::cuda_is_available()) "cuda" else "cpu")
model$to(device = device)

print(model)

title: Simple audio classification with torch
text:
Model fitting
Unlike in tensorflow, there is no model %>% compile(...) step in torch, so we are going to set loss criterion, optimizer strategy and evaluation metrics explicitly in the training loop.

loss_criterion <- torch::nn_cross_entropy_loss()
optimizer <- torch::optim_adadelta(model$parameters, rho = 0.95, eps = 1e-7)
metrics <- list(acc = yardstick::accuracy_vec)


Training loop

library(glue)
library(progress)

pred_to_r <- function(x) {
  classes <- factor(df$classes)
  classes[as.numeric(x$to(device = "cpu"))]
}

set_progress_bar <- function(total) {
  progress_bar$new(
    total = total, clear = FALSE, width = 70,
    format = ":current/:total [:bar] - :elapsed - loss: :loss - acc: :acc"
  )
}


epochs <- 20
losses <- c()
accs <- c()

for(epoch in seq_len(epochs)) {
  pb <- set_progress_bar(length(ds_train))
  pb$message(glue("Epoch {epoch}/{epochs}"))
  coro::loop(for(batch in ds_train) {
    optimizer$zero_grad()
    predictions <- model(batch[[1]]$to(device = device))
    targets <- batch[[2]]$to(device = device)
    loss <- loss_criterion(predictions, targets)
    loss$backward()
    optimizer$step()
    
    # eval reports
    prediction_r <- pred_to_r(predictions$argmax(dim = 2))
    targets_r <- pred_to_r(targets)
    acc <- metrics$acc(targets_r, prediction_r)
    accs <- c(accs, acc)
    loss_r <- as.numeric(loss$item())
    losses <- c(losses, loss_r)
    
    pb$tick(tokens = list(loss = round(mean(losses), 4), acc = round(mean(accs), 4)))
  })
}



# test
predictions_r <- c()
targets_r <- c()
coro::loop(for(batch_test in ds_test) {
  predictions <- model(batch_test[[1]]$to(device = device))
  targets <- batch_test[[2]]$to(device = device)
  predictions_r <- c(predictions_r, pred_to_r(predictions$argmax(dim = 2)))
  targets_r <- c(targets_r, pred_to_r(targets))
})
