title: targetsboard 0.1.0: a live view of your {targets} pipeline
text:
A {targets} pipeline makes an analysis easier to reproduce: each target is a named step, dependencies form a graph, and cached results let tar_make() focus work where it is needed. But when a pipeline is running, it can still be useful to see its state, understand what changed, and trace a warning or error back to the code that produced it.
That is the problem I wanted to explore with targetsboard, a graphical companion for authors of {targets} pipelines. I have released its first version, v0.1.0. This post is a short introduction for researchers, data scientists and data engineers who already use targets or are curious about making analytical workflows easier to inspect and operate.
The package is still experimental and at an early stage. The board is intended to help you understand a pipeline while working on it; it does not replace the pipeline script, the store, version control, or the decisions that make an analysis reproducible.

title: targetsboard 0.1.0: a live view of your {targets} pipeline
text:
What the board shows
targetsboard draws the pipeline as a directed graph. Nodes show whether targets are up to date, outdated, running or in error. Focus a target to see its place in the dependency graph and preview its value. The board also surfaces warnings and errors, with supporting information such as a traceback and code you can use to reproduce or debug a target.



targetsboard while a pipeline is running: target statuses are visible in the graph, and the selected problem shows its error, traceback and reproducible code in the side pane.


This view connects a few familiar reproducibility and MLOps concerns to the work of an R analysis: lineage is visible in the dependency graph, run status is visible as work progresses, and debugging context is attached to the target that needs attention. The graph is a way to inspect the pipeline, not a substitute for recording code, data inputs and environment details in your project.

title: targetsboard 0.1.0: a live view of your {targets} pipeline
section: Try it with an existing project
text:
Try it with an existing project
Install the released package from GitHub:
remotes::install_github("Athospd/targetsboard@v0.1.0")
Open an R session in a project that already has a {targets} pipeline, then start the board:
library(targetsboard)

app <- tar_board()
tar_board() starts the board in a background R process and opens it in your browser. It uses the targets script and store configured for the current project, just as tar_watch() does. You can then run the pipeline from R as usual:
targets::tar_make()
As targets run, watch their statuses update on the graph. Select a node to inspect its dependencies and value. If something warns or errors, open its problem details to review the message and traceback, then use the provided code to reproduce the target or start a debug run.
You can also start a run from the board. Run all builds the pipeline; target menus and selection let you run or invalidate a target, or work with a group. The Problems and Log tabs collect issues and output from the latest board run. The board’s run controls include options to continue after errors or treat warnings as errors, which can help reveal multiple issues or stop at a warning with a debugging workspace.
When you are finished, close the board with its power button or stop its background process from R:
app$kill()
The pipeline remains defined by your targets project. targetsboard does not silently rewrite _targets.R; the controls start runs or invalidation through targets and help you inspect what happened. This keeps the project script as the place to review how the analysis is built.

text:
See it in action
The short demo follows a pipeline run, changes the graph layout, previews target values, and finds, fixes and rebuilds after an error:



Watch the targetsboard demo on YouTube

title: targetsboard 0.1.0: a live view of your {targets} pipeline
text:
First release, early project
Version 0.1.0 turns an earlier prototype into a board for following and operating a pipeline during development. It includes graph and status views, target and group actions, problem and run logs, value previews, and debugging support. It also remembers graph layout and includes example pipelines for trying different situations.
This is the first release, not a claim that every workflow or large pipeline is covered. The repository describes the package as experimental and notes that performance and usability still need work. If you try it, please share issues and ideas on GitHub. The code and installation instructions are in the targetsboard repository.

title: targetfy: turn your R scripts into a {targets} pipeline
text:
I like {targets}. It made the top 4 of my 2026 package list. But most of my R code doesn’t start as a pipeline. It starts as a script, analysis.R, that I run top to bottom, and it grows. By the time I’d like caching, the work to rewrite it is enough to keep putting it off.
So I wrote targetfy, a skill for Claude Code that does the rewrite for me. You point it at your scripts and it writes the equivalent {targets} pipeline. This is the first post about it, so here’s what it does and how to try it.

title: targetfy: turn your R scripts into a {targets} pipeline
text:
Why {targets}?
If you haven’t used it: {targets} turns your analysis into a graph of steps, the targets, and remembers each step’s result. When you change something, tar_make() reruns only the steps that depend on the change and skips the rest. A model that takes an hour doesn’t refit because you changed a plot’s title.

title: targetfy: turn your R scripts into a {targets} pipeline
text:
A small example
Here’s a typical script:
rm(list = ls())
setwd("C:/my/project")
library(stats)
df <- read.csv("data/sales.csv")
df <- df[df$year > 2020, ]
df$rev <- log(df$rev)
model <- lm(rev ~ region, df)
print(summary(model))
model_summary <- summary(model)$coefficients
dir.create("out", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(model_summary, "out/coefs.csv")
Ask Claude Code to “targetify analysis.R”, or type /targetfy, and you get a _targets.R:
library(targets)
library(tarchetypes)
tar_source("R")
tar_option_set(packages = c("stats"))
list(
  tar_file_read(sales, "data/sales.csv", read = read.csv(!!.x)),
  tar_target(sales_clean, clean_sales(sales)),
  tar_target(model, fit_model(sales_clean)),
  tar_target(model_summary, summarise_model(model)),
  tar_file(coefs_file, write_coefs(model_summary, "out/coefs.csv"))
)
and the functions behind it, in R/analysis_functions.R:
clean_sales <- function(sales) {
  sales <- sales[sales$year > 2020, ]
  sales$rev <- log(sales$rev)
  sales
}

fit_model <- function(sales_clean) lm(rev ~ region, sales_clean)

summarise_model <- function(model) summary(model)$coefficients

write_coefs <- function(model_summary, path) {
  dir.create(dirname(path), showWarnings = FALSE)
  write.csv(model_summary, path)
  path
}
A few things happened along the way:

The three lines that build and clean df became one step, sales_clean. A step is a meaningful object (a dataset, a model, a summary, a file), not every assignment.
Steps got names that say what they hold (sales_clean, not df), and their functions got verbs (clean_sales()).
The input CSV is tracked, so editing data/sales.csv reruns everything downstream. The output CSV is tracked as a file too.
rm(list = ls()), setwd() and print() were dropped: they don’t belong in a pipeline. Each dropped line is listed, with the reason, in a report.

title: targetfy: turn your R scripts into a {targets} pipeline
text:
It checks its own work
This is the part I care most about. A rewrite that looks right isn’t enough, so targetfy doesn’t decide on its own that the pipeline is correct. A bundled R script runs your original scripts and the new pipeline, each in a throwaway copy of the project, and compares the results: the final objects and the files written. The conversion is accepted only when they match. If they don’t, Claude reads what differs, fixes the pipeline and tries again.
It also never touches your files. Your scripts, data and renv.lock stay as they are; targetfy only adds the pipeline, the functions, and the report next to them. If you already have a _targets.R, it writes targets_analysis.R with its own store instead, so your existing pipeline’s cache is safe. And it installs nothing: if a package is missing, it tells you.
At the end, it runs tar_glimpse() and shows you the pipeline’s graph. This is the real one for the example above:

title: targetfy: turn your R scripts into a {targets} pipeline
text:
Then, optionally, make it faster
Once the pipeline passes the check, targetfy offers improvements one at a time, each tied to a specific step. You can say no to all of them:

Storage formats, such as qs2 or parquet, for big objects.
Dynamic branching, when a step loops over groups, files or parameters, so each branch caches on its own.
Parallel workers with {crew}, when steps can run at the same time.

Each one is checked again. If an improvement changes the results, it’s undone.

title: targetfy: turn your R scripts into a {targets} pipeline
text:
Try it
You need Claude Code and R with targets, tarchetypes, callr and jsonlite. Install the skill with:
git clone https://github.com/Athospd/targetfy.git ~/.claude/skills/targetfy
Then open your project in Claude Code and ask it to convert your script, or a sequence of scripts in run order (01_load.R, 02_model.R, …). When one script saves an .rds that the next one reads, that becomes a direct link between steps.
For now it supports plain .R files. R Markdown and Quarto documents are planned.
It’s new, so I’d love to hear how it does on your scripts. Issues and ideas are welcome on GitHub.

title: Top 10 packages for data science
text:
R has changed a lot in the last 5 years thanks to new packages focused on the most practical, day-to-day problems of a data scientist. Below is my top 10 of the packages that revolutionized the way of programming in R and made my work faster and more enjoyable:

10. purrr (vector and list manipulation)
Our tenth place has put the for loop at risk of extinction. With it, applying functions over vectors, lists or combinations of both takes a few lines and no confusing i, j, k indices. And with the arrival of tibbles, your data.frames can now hold much more than mere numbers and strings, and purrr is your strongest ally when creating the so-called list-columns.


9. caret (statistical modeling)
If you are after statistical modeling (a basic tool of the data scientist), give caret a chance. This package brings together the most established predictive modeling algorithms (aka machine learning) ever made in R, and it also implements the typical tools of the model building process, for example cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, train/test sets, preprocessing and even parallelization. Besides the different model fitting techniques, their diagnostics and visualizations were also conveniently gathered, all in one place, which makes searching for parts in R’s gigantic bucket less costly.


8. knitr/rmarkdown (reports)
The knitr and rmarkdown duo turned R from ugly duckling into the king of the spotlight. After them, reports in R are easy, pretty and flexible. Writing in RMarkdown is like writing a draft that is later turned into a decent file in any format: pdf, word and html are the most common. The idea behind RMarkdown is to bring the focus to the analysis and leave the frills in the background as much as possible.
PS: every post on this blog is made with RMarkdown!


7. stringr (string manipulation)
Stringr gives you everything to extract, create and transform strings. Its functions accept regex, extremely versatile and efficient. Text mining becomes child’s play.


6. lubridate (date manipulation)
If there is one thing that can give you an endless headache, it’s dates. That’s why lubridate was invented. Everything you’d like to do with dates and times this package provides, from addition and subtraction to logical comparisons and rounding. It’s the ideal tool for dealing with time.


5. shiny (web apps)
Shiny gives a data analyst the power to build web applications without any prior knowledge of html, css and javascript. Believe it or not, building interactive, data-driven websites is no longer exclusive to web developers. With a slightly long learning curve, you can create anything from static dashboards to custom maps à la google maps! It’s a great way to present results and works very well as the final product of management tools.


4. tidyr (reshaping data.frames)
Its main functions are gather() and spread(). They pivot/unpivot data.frames, or melt/cast data.frames. It deserves our fourth place because it has great synergy with the third and second places. Quite often we need to rearrange a set of columns into a pair of key/value columns or vice versa. Pivoting/unpivoting is particularly annoying to do in SQL, and tidyr makes it look trivial. It also has other useful functions that I recommend checking out (e.g. unite(), separete()).


3. dplyr (data.frame manipulation)
Our bronze medal goes to dplyr because it brought the data manipulation verbs to the simplest and most intuitive level. They are:

filter() filters rows
arrange() sorts rows
select() selects columns
distinct() removes duplicated rows
mutate() builds new columns
group_by() + summarise() summarises values by one or more factors

And the package goes far beyond these verbs. It’s worth exploring its functions if you need to get your dataset ready for analysis.
PS: it was made to work with the “pipe” (%>%).


2. ggplot2 (visualization)
The silver medal goes to what I think is the most famous R package.
R is known for its rich graphics capabilities, but it was ggplot2 that brought the joy of living to users who care even a little about how their visualizations look. ggplot2 lets you use the grammar of graphics to build layered, customizable plots. There is a small learning curve, but the time invested pays off with the first plot you make. Plots that would be true feats of engineering in base R take no more than 5 lines of ggplot2, and they look prettier too!
A must in any data scientist’s toolbox.


1. magrittr (pipe!)
The gold medal gives us the famous pipe (%>%). Instead of h(g(f(x))), write x %>% f %>% g %>% h. That’s it! That’s all the pipe does. You may wonder why on earth this deserves our first place, but believe me: the pipe is revolutionary. It changed the way of programming in R. The gain in code readability and programming speed is unimaginable. And it opened the door to packages that wouldn’t be viable without it, including dplyr and tidyr.
That’s why it deserves first place on our list and a spot in our page’s logo.


Honorable mentions
Other packages also deserve a highlight! The honorable mention medals go to:

forcats (factor utilities)
Rcpp (R to C++)
FactoMiner (multivariate analysis)
RODBC (database connection)
httr/xml2/rvest (web tools)
flexdashboard (rmarkdown in dashboard format)
janitor (data cleaning for modeling)
plyr (manipulation of vectors, lists and data.frames)
roxygen2 (R package creation)
devtools (miscellaneous tools)
htmlwidgets (integration between R and JavaScript libraries)
leaflet (interactive maps)

What about you, do you agree? Tell us in the comments which packages live in your heart! =)

text:
Initial guess
Julião has already been working on this problem and took an initial shot at the code for you to get inspired. Well, “initial” is a stretch, because he went straight to a CNN with the help of the decryptr package:

library(keras)
library(tidyverse)
library(decryptr)

path <- "."
arqs <- dir(paste0(path,  "/train_imgs"), full.names = TRUE)
resp <- readr::read_csv(paste0(path,  "/train_responses.csv"))

i_train <- sample(1:nrow(resp), 10000)
arqs_train <- arqs[i_train]
arqs_test <- arqs[-i_train]

gen <- function(batch_size = 100, arqs = arqs_train) {
  f <- function() {
    a <- sort(sample(arqs, batch_size))
    imgs <- decryptr::read_captcha(a)
    captchas_t <- purrr::transpose(imgs)
    xs <- captchas_t$x
    xs <- abind::abind(xs, along = 0.1)
    a_clean <- a %>% 
      basename() %>% 
      tools::file_path_sans_ext() %>% 
      tolower()
    corr <- resp %>% 
      filter(id %in% a_clean) %>% 
      arrange(id) %>% 
      pull(corr)
    data <- list(xs, corr)
    data
  }
  f
}


# Create model
model <- keras_model_sequential()
model %>%
  layer_conv_2d(
    input_shape = c(150, 150, 1),
    filters = 16, kernel_size = c(3, 3),
    padding = "same",
    activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_max_pooling_2d() %>%
  layer_conv_2d(
    filters = 32, kernel_size = c(3, 3),
    padding = "same",
    activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_max_pooling_2d() %>%
  layer_conv_2d(
    filters = 64, kernel_size = c(3, 3),
    padding = "same",
    activation = "relu") %>%
  layer_max_pooling_2d() %>%
  layer_flatten() %>%
  layer_dense(units = 300) %>%
  layer_dropout(.1) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "tanh")


# Compile and fit model
model %>%
  compile(
    optimizer = "sgd",
    loss = "mean_squared_error",
    metrics = "mean_squared_error")

model %>%
  fit_generator(
    gen(100, arqs_train),
    steps_per_epoch = 100,
    validation_data = gen(100, arqs_test),
    validation_steps = 10
  )

So? Can you get it 100% right? Or is it impossible?
Happy R’ing!

title: Top 10 packages for data science, 2026 edition
text: In 2017 I wrote my top 10 packages for data science. Nine years later, some of them are still on my list, some were replaced by their successors, and some new ones changed the way I work. Here is the 2026 edition, plus a special mention for the packages of the GenAI era.

title: Top 10 packages for data science, 2026 edition
text:
What the downloads say
A top 10 is a matter of taste, but the download counts are data. The CRAN logs of Posit’s mirror are public, so here are the 2017 list and the 2026 list, with downloads in the month before each post.

library(tidyverse)
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")

downloads <- function(pkgs, from, to) {
  url <- str_glue("https://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/downloads/total/{from}:{to}/{str_flatten(pkgs, ',')}")
  jsonlite::fromJSON(url) |> select(package, downloads)
}

top_2017 <- c("magrittr", "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "shiny", "lubridate", "stringr", "rmarkdown", "caret", "purrr")
top_2026 <- c("torch", "ggplot2", "tidyverse", "targets", "shiny", "lubridate", "mirai", "quarto", "tidymodels", "purrr")

pkgs <- union(top_2017, top_2026)

bind_rows(
  feb_2017 = downloads(pkgs, "2017-01-21", "2017-02-20"),
  nov_2026 = downloads(pkgs, "2026-10-20", "2026-11-18"),
  .id = "month"
) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = month, values_from = downloads) |>
  mutate(
    feb_2017 = na_if(feb_2017, 0), # torch, targets, tidymodels, quarto and mirai didn't exist yet
    rank_2017 = match(package, top_2017),
    rank_2026 = match(package, top_2026)
  ) |>
  arrange(rank_2026, rank_2017) |>
